answer.exemplar: The flag was a good decision when it was made, because it let a risky change be narrowed and then turned off within a minute. Two years on, that is no longer what it is. It is a permanent branch evaluated on every request, so it is on the hot path forever; it is code nobody has executed, so the path most likely to run in an emergency is the one nobody can test; and it is a second answer to every question the code asks, so every future change has to reason about both branches and a reader has to work out which one is live. Deleting the code it guarded would have been cheaper than keeping it, which is the point: a flag has a shelf life and nothing enforces it. The discipline that ends this is an owner and a removal date at the moment the flag is created, a ticket that appears when the date passes, and a review that treats a flag older than its release as a defect rather than a safety feature.

answer.exemplar: The rare fault is rare because the code path that produces it is unusual, and the reason it is hard to find is that the ordinary records are not what you need. Turning every line to debug looks like the answer and is the opposite, for three reasons that compound. The first is volume: at a few thousand requests a second, extra lines per request become hundreds of gigabytes a day, which costs money, slows the indexing that makes logs searchable at all, and pushes the interesting days out of the retention window. The second is signal: the lines that explain the rare fault are now mixed with millions of near-identical ones, so the one record you need is harder to isolate than when it was the only unusual thing in the file. The third is that a log level is a global dial, so it cannot be turned up for the one request being investigated. The workable alternative is to make the ordinary record complete enough to explain the rare one, meaning a request identifier and the identifiers it depends on on every request, and to add targeted fields to that one path. Ask the question first, log the answer, leave the level alone.

answer.exemplar: A region is not a label on a service; it is a place where a disk, a backup and a support engineer are. Committing to a region therefore commits to three things at once, and the first is legal exposure, which is the constraint being written down. A record held in one country is subject to that country's law whatever encrypts it, and that holds for a backup as surely as for a live row, so a copy written across the border breaks the commitment on the night it is written rather than the night it is used. The second is operational: a promise that can be broken by a routine job is a promise that will be broken, because the runbook author will have assumed the primary region was the only thing that mattered. The third is that the constraint outlives the architecture, so a later region, a new backup target or a disaster recovery exercise can each break it quietly. The discipline is to enumerate every place a record can be written, including snapshots, replicas, log archives and test environments, and check each against the list, and to make the residency rule something the deployment tooling refuses rather than something a runbook remembers.

answer.exemplar: Naming a person as the cause records that a decision was made, and the system is still perfectly able to make that decision again, so the failure remains available to the next person on the same rota. It also stops the investigation early: once someone is at fault the review has an answer, and the search for the missing signal ends. A person cannot be made to act differently at 4am by a document, but a system can be given a reason to stop. What such a finding has to name instead is the condition that made the mistake easy and invisible: the dashboard that existed but was not watched, the check that would have caught it, the bound that would have stopped the growth, the runbook step that would have shortened the page, or the review that should have required a test. Blameless does not mean nobody was wrong, it means the subject of the sentence is the system rather than a colleague, which is what lets the action item be a thing that can be built, tested and dated.
